en: What it doesn't show: This is not proof that real fireflies tune their beats this way. Only some firefly species synchronize in nature, and this model reduces a flash to a single clock, without light intensity, field of view that depends on distance, or learning by the fireflies. It is not fitted to any particular observed data either.

A simplified implementation of the idea of pulse-coupled oscillators (Mirollo, Strogatz (1990), "Synchronization of pulse-coupled biological oscillators", SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 50(6)). It does not reproduce the paper's numbers; it is this project's own design.

Phase counts one cycle as 1 and grows by 0.02 per step. Each firefly's speed is normally distributed with mean 1 and a standard deviation equal to the "speed spread." When a firefly flashes, the phase of neighbors in range is increased by the coupling strength, and any that pass 1 flash in the same step.

With the default settings (coupling 2.5%, range 30%, speed spread 10%), 10 seeds all reach synchrony (r>0.9), taking 2 to 31 cycles (mostly 2 to 6). At coupling of 1% or less r stays below 0.2, and at 3% or more it is near 0.95 (verify with node tools/validate-firefly.js).
Graphs ④ and ⑤ change only the given value in the same setup, run 30 cycles 3 times each, and show the average r of the last 6 cycles.
The code is available on GitHub.
Can Monkeys Write Hamlet? · Simulatio Lab
Could monkeys typing random letters write a line of Hamlet? Compare pure chance with cumulative selection yourself.

The "infinite monkey theorem" says that a monkey hitting typewriter keys at random will eventually produce Hamlet. But how long is "eventually"? Here is a race toward the same target, one side by pure chance and one by selection that improves little by little.
The symbols are the 26 uppercase letters plus the space, 27 in all, and the target is a line from Hamlet (TO BE OR NOT TO BE or METHINKS IT IS LIKE A WEASEL).
Pure chance: at every step, 5,000 completely random sentences are typed and the one matching the target in the most places is recorded. Earlier results have no influence on later attempts.

Cumulative selection: start from one random sentence; each generation makes copies and changes each letter with some probability. The sentence (parent included) matching the target in the most places becomes the next generation's parent. The difference is that correct letters are carried over.
Both methods are scored only by "how many letters match the target." Highlighted letter boxes are the ones that match.

What it shows: For chance trying to hit the target in one go, the expected number of attempts grows 27-fold with every added letter, which makes it practically impossible. Cumulative selection, which keeps the letters it got right, reaches the same sentence in a few thousand attempts. Even with the same randomness, "getting everything right at once" and "building up step by step" are completely different things.

What it doesn't show: It does not mean real biological evolution works like this program. The model has a preset target sentence, whereas evolution has no set goal, a point Dawkins himself made. This experiment only shows the difference in power between "chance that must hit in one go" and "selection that filters at every step." It is also not a claim about whether monkeys could actually write Hamlet.

This is this project's own implementation, inspired by the thought experiment known as the "infinite monkey theorem" and by the "weasel program" Richard Dawkins described in The Blind Watchmaker (1986). It is not a literal port of the program in the book.

The targets are lines from Hamlet: "To be, or not to be" (Act 3, Scene 1) and "Methinks it is like a weasel" (Act 3, Scene 2). The symbols are the 26 uppercase letters and the space; punctuation such as commas is left out.

With the default settings (100 copies, 5% mutation), 20 runs took on average 46 generations (min 26, max 89) for TO BE OR NOT TO BE and 77 generations (min 43, max 116) for METHINKS IT IS LIKE A WEASEL. After a million attempts, chance had matched only about 7/18 and 9/28.

The expected number of attempts to hit an L-letter sentence by chance in one go is 27<sup>L</sup>. "One billion attempts per second" is this project's assumption, and the age of the universe is taken as about 13.8 billion years. For 18 letters that is about 1.8 billion years (0.13 times the age of the universe); for 28 letters, about 3.8×10<sup>23</sup> years.

For very short sentences (1 to 2 letters), cumulative selection with these settings is actually slower than chance, because with only 5% of letters changing, even 100 copies rarely differ. You can verify with node tools/validate-monkey.js.
The code is available on GitHub.
What If 100 AI Painters Copy Each Other? · Simulatio Lab
What happens to the diversity of styles when painters copy each other? Change the copy rate and originality and run it yourself.

One hundred painters look at each other's work and copy the styles they like. How do paintings that start out all different change? Vary how often they copy and how original they are, and look for the point where everything converges on a single style.
